illustrations.title: The Father Who Ran
illustrations.text: In the ancient Near East a grown man of standing did not run. To run, he would gather the long folds of his robe in his hands and bare his legs, and that was a thing for boys and slaves, not for fathers with land. So when Jesus says the father saw his son a long way off and ran to him, the first hearers would have felt the shock of it. The father shamed himself in the road. He took the disgrace that belonged to the boy and wore it in public before the son could say a word.
illustrations.point: Grace is not God waiting at the gate with arms crossed. It is God taking on our shame in the open road before we have finished our apology.

illustrations.title: The Tab Already Paid
illustrations.text: A man sat down at a diner counter, ordered a full meal, and ate slowly, dreading the bill the whole time because his wallet was nearly empty. When he asked for the check the waitress told him a stranger two stools down had already covered it and left. He had eaten the entire meal under a weight that was never real. The debt was settled before he tasted the first bite. He just did not know it.
illustrations.point: Most of us live as though the bill is still ours to pay. The cross says it was settled before we sat down.

illustrations.title: Not a Fuel Card
illustrations.text: We tend to treat grace like a fuel card we swipe when the tank runs low. We sin, we run dry, we come back for a top up, and we go again. But grace was never meant to be the thing that gets us back on the road we were already driving. It is meant to put us in a different car going a different direction. The point of being forgiven is not to keep doing the thing more comfortably.
illustrations.point: Grace that only relieves guilt and changes nothing else has been misread. Real grace rebuilds the life, not just the conscience.

illustrations.title: The Mended Coat
illustrations.text: A boy tore his good coat climbing a fence he had been told to stay off. He hid it in the back of the closet for weeks, ashamed. When his grandmother finally found it she did not lecture. She sat by the lamp for two evenings and stitched the tear so carefully that the seam became the strongest part of the cloth. He wore that coat for years, and the place he broke was the place that never tore again.
illustrations.point: God does not merely overlook the broken place. He mends it into the strongest part of the life.

illustrations.title: The Judge Who Paid
illustrations.text: There is an old story told of a judge whose own friend came before his bench, guilty and unable to pay the fine. The courtroom waited to see whether friendship would bend the law. The judge pronounced the full penalty, every dollar of it, because the law is the law. Then he stepped down from the bench, took out his own wallet, and paid the fine himself. Justice was not waved away. It was satisfied, and then it was carried by the one who handed it down.
illustrations.point: God does not lower the demand of justice to forgive us. He meets it in full and then pays it Himself.

illustrations.title: The Neighbor's Laundry
illustrations.text: A woman watched her neighbor hang laundry every morning and complained that the wash always looked dingy and gray. She said it for weeks. One day the lines came out bright and clean, and she remarked that the neighbor had finally learned to wash properly. Her husband said quietly that nothing had changed next door. He had simply gotten up early and cleaned their own window.
illustrations.point: What looks like everyone else's failure is often the grime on the glass we are looking through. Repentance starts by washing our own window.

illustrations.title: The Small Leak
illustrations.text: No ship sinks from the wave that crests the deck in the storm. Ships sink from the slow leak no one bothered to fix in calm water, the seam that wept a little each day until the hold was full. The sailors who survive are not the ones who fear the storm most. They are the ones who check the hull when the sea is flat and nothing seems wrong.
illustrations.point: Sin rarely drowns us in a single dramatic wave. It is the small unconfessed leak in calm seasons that fills the hold.

illustrations.title: The Sin I Managed
illustrations.text: There is a kind of sin a pastor learns to manage rather than kill. You build a fence around it. You set rules. You tell yourself the fence is holding. And for years it does, until a hard season leans on the fence and you discover you never actually wanted the thing dead, you only wanted it contained where it would not embarrass you. Management is not repentance. I have confused the two in my own heart more than once.
illustrations.point: Containing a sin so it stays presentable is not the same as repenting of it. God asks for the death of the thing, not its careful management.

illustrations.title: Two Degrees Off
illustrations.text: A pilot who sets out across the ocean two degrees off course will not notice the error for an hour. The plane feels level. The instruments hum. But two degrees held over a thousand miles does not land you slightly off the runway. It lands you in a different country entirely. The danger was never the size of the error. It was the distance over which a small error was allowed to run uncorrected.
illustrations.point: A small sin tolerated is not small over time. The drift compounds, and uncorrected it lands you somewhere you never meant to be.

illustrations.title: The Weeds at the Fence
illustrations.text: Anyone who has kept a garden knows the weeds you can see are not the problem. You pull those in an afternoon. The problem is the root system running under the soil where you cannot reach, sending up new shoots faster than you can bend down. Cutting the green off the top makes the yard look tended for a week. It does nothing to the thing that is actually growing.
illustrations.point: Behavior management cuts the green off the top. Repentance goes after the root, which only God can reach.

illustrations.title: Anvil and Hammer
illustrations.text: An old blacksmith was asked how many hammers he had worn out over his years at the forge. He laughed and said he had never worn out a hammer. He had worn out a great many anvils, because the anvil takes every blow while the hammer only delivers it. At the cross God did not stand back and swing the hammer of justice at us. He laid Himself on the anvil and took every blow the hammer fell.
illustrations.point: On the cross God did not deliver the blow of judgment from a safe distance. He absorbed it in His own body.

illustrations.title: The Electric Chair on a Chain
illustrations.text: We hang crosses on chains of gold and set them on steeples and stitch them into the covers of our finest books. We have made the cross beautiful. But in the first century the cross was a thing of horror, the empire's most public and degrading way to kill a man, reserved for slaves and rebels. To wear one then would have been like wearing a small golden noose or a tiny gallows around your neck. We forget what we are looking at.
illustrations.point: The cross is not a piece of religious decoration. It is an instrument of execution that God turned into the place of our rescue.

illustrations.title: The Bridge of One Body
illustrations.text: There is an old account of a railway switchman whose own son wandered onto the tracks just as a train full of passengers came around the bend. To save the train he had to lower the bridge, and lowering the bridge would crush the boy below. He could save the many or save the one. He chose the train, and watched it pass over his son, and the passengers never looked up from their newspapers, never knowing the cost of their safe arrival.
illustrations.point: We pass over the cross every day without looking up from our lives. A Father gave a Son, and we ride on the safety it bought.

illustrations.title: Into the Wilderness
illustrations.text: On the Day of Atonement in ancient Israel the high priest laid both hands on the head of a goat and confessed over it the sins of the whole nation. Then the goat was led out into the wilderness, carrying what belonged to the people, until it was gone past seeing and would not return. The people watched their guilt walk away from them over the horizon. They did not chase it. They let it go.
illustrations.point: Christ is the one who carries our guilt out past return. The cross means the sin does not come back over the horizon.

illustrations.title: The Curtain Torn
illustrations.text: In the temple a heavy curtain sealed off the holiest place, and only one man entered, once a year, after blood and ritual, into the presence of God. The curtain was a closed door that said stay out. When Jesus died the Gospels tell us that curtain tore from top to bottom, not bottom to top, as though torn by a hand reaching down rather than up. The door no man could open from his side was opened from God's.
illustrations.point: The way into God's presence was never something we could force open. At the cross God tore it open from His side.

illustrations.title: Stained Glass Needs the Dark
illustrations.text: Stained glass in a great cathedral is nothing in a lit room. Walk past it with the lamps on and it is dull, gray, almost ugly. The glass only does what it was made to do when the light comes from outside and the room itself is dark. Then every color burns and the whole window tells its story. The darkness in the room is not the enemy of the picture. It is the condition under which the picture can finally be seen.
illustrations.point: Some things God means to show us only become visible in the dark. The suffering is not the ruin of the picture but the room in which it is finally seen.

illustrations.title: Grief Is Not Doubt
illustrations.text: A woman sat in my office months after burying her husband, ashamed that she still wept, certain that her grief meant her faith had failed. I asked her whether she thought the depth of her sorrow was a measure of how much she had loved him. She said yes, of course. Then I asked why she would think God was offended by the size of a wound that was simply the size of her love.
illustrations.point: Deep grief is not a failure of faith. It is the cost of having loved, and God does not require us to feel a loss less than it is.

illustrations.title: Trees Grown in Wind
illustrations.text: When researchers built sealed domes to grow trees in perfect conditions, with steady light and no weather, the trees grew fast and then fell over. They lacked what foresters call stress wood, the dense fiber a tree lays down when the wind bends it. A tree that is never pushed against never grows the strength to stand. The wind it fights is the very thing that lets it hold its own weight when it is tall.
illustrations.point: A life never pushed against grows brittle. The resistance we resent is often what God uses to make us able to stand.

illustrations.title: Gold in the Cracks
illustrations.text: There is an old craft in Japan called kintsugi, the mending of broken pottery with lacquer mixed with gold. The artist does not hide the break. He fills the fracture with gold so that the seam becomes the most beautiful and valuable part of the bowl. The piece is not returned to what it was. It is made into something the unbroken bowl could never have been. The history of its breaking is written across it in gold.
illustrations.point: God does not restore us to who we were before the breaking. He fills the fracture with something the unbroken life could never have held.

illustrations.title: The Mercy of the Fever
illustrations.text: A fever feels like the illness, but it is the body's defense, the heat that makes you miserable while it burns out the thing that would kill you. We curse the fever and beg for it to break, not understanding that the discomfort is the fight, not the disease. There are seasons of pain that work the same way in a soul. The thing that feels like it is wrecking us is the very heat doing the saving work.
illustrations.point: Not all of our pain is the disease. Some of it is the cure, and God does not always break the fever when we ask.

illustrations.title: Thomas Stayed in the Room
illustrations.text: We call him Doubting Thomas as though doubt were the whole of him. But notice where his doubt kept him. It kept him in the room. A week after he said he would not believe without seeing the wounds, he was still there with the others, still gathered, still close enough that when Jesus came he was present to be met. His doubt did not drive him out the door. It held him in the place where faith could find him.
illustrations.point: Honest doubt that stays in the room is not the enemy of faith. It is the doubt that walks out the door we should fear.

illustrations.title: Help My Unbelief
illustrations.text: A father brought his sick son to Jesus and said the strangest prayer in the Gospels. I believe, he said, help my unbelief. In a single breath he confessed faith and confessed its weakness. He did not wait to get his certainty in order before he came. He brought the faith he had, thin and mixed with fear, and he handed the whole tangled thing to Jesus and asked Him to make up the difference.
illustrations.point: You do not have to resolve your doubt before you bring it to God. Bring the faith you have and ask Him to make up the rest.

illustrations.title: Ice on the Pond
illustrations.text: A child and a seasoned skater can both cross the same frozen pond. The child inches out trembling, sure the ice will crack with every step. The skater glides over it without a thought. Their confidence is wildly different, but they arrive at the same far shore, because what carries them is not the strength of their faith. It is the thickness of the ice. Weak faith in solid ice still crosses the pond.
illustrations.point: We are not saved by the strength of our faith but by the strength of the One we trust. Thin faith in a solid Christ still arrives.

illustrations.title: Questions in the House
illustrations.text: There is a difference between a child who asks his father hard questions across the dinner table and a child who slams the door and asks the questions of strangers on the street. The questions may be word for word the same. What differs is whether they are asked inside the relationship or after leaving it. The church has often punished honest questions and so taught its children to take them outside, where no one who loves them gets to answer.
illustrations.point: Doubt asked inside the relationship with God is not rebellion. The tragedy is a church that drives its questioners out to ask elsewhere.

illustrations.title: What Happens in the Cocoon
illustrations.text: Inside the cocoon the caterpillar does not simply sprout wings. It dissolves. Its body breaks down almost entirely into a kind of living soup, and from that undoing the butterfly is built according to a pattern that was hidden in it all along. If you opened the cocoon halfway through, you would find what looks like death and ruin. You would not guess that the dissolving was the way to the wings.
illustrations.point: What looks like the end and the undoing of us is, in God's hands, the means of a body we cannot yet picture.

illustrations.title: Gone From Our Sight
illustrations.text: Stand on the shore and watch a ship sail out until it is a speck on the horizon and then nothing at all. Gone, you say. But the ship has not grown smaller. It is the same size, with the same cargo and the same souls aboard, and at that very moment on a far shore other voices are crying out that here she comes. Our gone is someone else's arrival. The horizon is the limit of our eyes, not the end of the ship.
illustrations.point: Death is the horizon, the limit of our sight, not the end of the one we love. On the far shore there is a welcome.

illustrations.title: The Seed in the Ground
illustrations.text: A farmer who buries seed in the autumn is not throwing it away, though to an outsider it looks like loss. He takes good grain, grain he could have eaten, and he covers it with dirt and walks away and lets it rot. Everyone who farms understands that the burying is not the end of the seed. It is the only door to the harvest. The grave of the seed is the beginning of the field.
illustrations.point: For the believer the grave is not a hole where life is lost. It is the ground where it is planted toward a harvest.

illustrations.title: Moving House
illustrations.text: When a family moves from an old house to a better one, the children sometimes grieve the only home they have known, the marks on the doorframe, the creak on the third stair. The parents do not grieve the same way, because they have seen the new house and know it is better in every room. The grief is real and the move is good at the same time. Both are true on the same afternoon.
illustrations.point: We grieve the only home we have known, and God does not scold the grief. But He has seen the house He is taking us to.

illustrations.title: Carried In Asleep
illustrations.text: A child falls asleep in the back of the car on a long drive home and wakes the next morning in his own bed, with no memory of being carried in. He did not arrive there by his own strength or staying awake. Stronger arms lifted him from the seat, carried him through the dark, laid him down, and pulled the covers up while he slept through all of it. He woke up home and safe and had done nothing but trust the one driving.
illustrations.point: The believer does not have to stay awake and strong to make the last passage. Stronger arms carry us through the dark and lay us down at home.

illustrations.title: The Child Who Asks for Everything
illustrations.text: A small child climbs into a father's lap and asks for things constantly, a snack, a toy, to be carried, to be told a story, with no sense at all that he is bothering the man. He has not yet learned to be embarrassed by his need. As we grow we lose that, and we start to ration our asking, certain we should not trouble God with the small things or the same thing twice. The child who asks for everything knows something about a father that we have forgotten.
illustrations.point: God is not wearied by our constant asking. We have grown too proud to need like children, and prayer calls us back to it.

illustrations.title: The Man Who Limped Away
illustrations.text: Jacob wrestled God by the river all night and would not let go until he was blessed. He got his blessing, but he also got something he did not ask for. He walked away with a limp that stayed with him the rest of his life. Real prayer is not a vending machine where you put in the words and get out the result unchanged. Sometimes you get what you wrestled for and a limp to remember the night you got it.
illustrations.point: Prayer that truly meets God does not leave us as we were. We may get the blessing and walk away marked by it.

illustrations.title: The Letters That Came Back
illustrations.text: A man kept a folder of prayers he felt God had ignored, requests sent up and never answered, and for years he read it as evidence that God was not listening. Late in life he opened the folder again and saw with clearer eyes that nearly every unanswered prayer had been a mercy. He had asked for things that would have wrecked him. The God he accused of silence had been protecting him by the very refusals he resented.
illustrations.point: Some of the prayers we count as unanswered were answered with a no that saved us. We thank Him for those last.

illustrations.title: The Line Stays Open
illustrations.text: When a child calls a parent and goes quiet, too upset or too tired to say anything, the parent does not hang up. They stay on the line in the silence, glad simply that the child called and is still there. There are seasons when we have no words to pray, when the well is dry and the sentences will not come. The silence is not the failure of prayer. The line is still open, and the One on the other end has not hung up.
illustrations.point: Wordless prayer is still prayer. God does not measure it by our eloquence but stays on the line through our silence.

illustrations.title: Why Counterfeits Exist
illustrations.text: No one counterfeits worthless paper. There are no forged three dollar bills, because forgery only follows real value. The counterfeit is always a copy of something genuine and good. Every idol works the same way. It is not evil because it imitates nothing. It is dangerous because it imitates something God made good, a love, a security, a glory, and offers it without the God it came from. The lie is powerful only because it is close to a truth.
illustrations.point: Idols are not random evils. They are good things from God that we have lifted into the place only God can hold.

illustrations.title: The Cargo Strapped to the Deck
illustrations.text: A ship can carry an enormous weight of cargo safely as long as the cargo stays in the hold, below the waterline, low and central. The trouble begins when the same good cargo is hauled up and strapped high on the deck. Now the very thing the ship was built to carry makes it top heavy, and the first hard wave rolls it over. The cargo did not change. Its weight did not change. Only its position did.
illustrations.point: Good things become idols not by being bad but by being lifted too high. A good love placed above God will capsize the soul.

illustrations.title: Drinking the Sea
illustrations.text: A sailor adrift and dying of thirst is surrounded by water he cannot drink. Salt water does not quench the thirst. It deepens it, and the more he drinks the more desperate his thirst becomes, until the very thing he reaches for to save himself is what kills him. Idols promise to satisfy a thirst and instead enlarge it. We come back to them more parched, certain that one more drink will finally do what the last hundred did not.
illustrations.point: An idol never satisfies the thirst it promises to end. It deepens the very ache it pretends to quench.

illustrations.title: The Day After the Win
illustrations.text: Athletes who spend a decade chasing a championship often describe the same strange emptiness the morning after they finally win it. The thing they organized their whole life around is achieved, the trophy is in their hands, and the hole they expected it to fill is still there, gaping and unchanged. The chase had hidden the emptiness. Arriving exposed it. The summit they climbed for years turned out to have nothing on it but the view of the next mountain.
illustrations.point: An idol cannot fill the hole it promised to fill, even when you finally reach it. Arrival exposes the lie the chase concealed.

illustrations.title: Carved by What Yields
illustrations.text: The deepest canyons on earth were not cut by anything hard. They were carved by water, the softest, most yielding thing, which does not fight the rock but goes around it and under it and keeps moving and keeps low. Given time, the thing that bends and stays low cuts deeper than any hammer. The rock that would not yield is gone. The water that always yielded is still running through the gorge it made.
illustrations.point: In God's economy it is not the hard and unbending that prevails. The one who stays low and yields outlasts the one who will not bend.

illustrations.title: Borrowed Light
illustrations.text: The moon lights the whole night sky and has not one watt of its own. Every bit of its brightness is borrowed from a sun on the far side of the earth, a sun the moon does not generate and cannot replace. The moon's only glory is to turn its face toward the light and reflect it down. The moment it forgot the borrowing and claimed the light as its own, it would have nothing to claim.
illustrations.point: Whatever light we shine is borrowed. Humility is simply remembering the source and refusing to bill it as our own.

illustrations.title: The Lowest Seat
illustrations.text: Jesus watched guests at a banquet scramble for the best seats and told them to do the opposite. Take the lowest place, He said, and let the host move you up rather than seat yourself high and be sent down in front of everyone. It was practical wisdom about dinner parties, and it was the architecture of the whole kingdom in one image. The way up runs through the bottom of the table. The one who grasps for the head seat has already lost it.
illustrations.point: In the kingdom the way up is down. The one who takes the lowest place is the one God lifts.

illustrations.title: Only the Empty Cup Fills
illustrations.text: A cup already full to the brim cannot receive a single drop more. Pour over it and the new water simply runs off the sides and is lost. The only cup that can be filled is the one that knows it is empty and holds itself out beneath the pitcher. This is why God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. It is not favoritism. It is the plain physics of a cup. The full self has no room for the gift.
illustrations.point: God gives grace to the humble because only the empty hands are open to receive. The full self has no room for the gift.

illustrations.title: Two Oars
illustrations.text: A man in a rowboat with two oars decided one morning that he would only pull the right oar, because that was the one he was good at, and the left one was his wife's job. He pulled hard and well, and the boat went in slow circles all afternoon and never left the cove. A boat does not move because one person rows hard. It moves because two people pull together against the same water in the same direction.
illustrations.point: A marriage where each rows only their own oar goes in circles. It moves only when two pull together against the same water.

illustrations.title: The Vow Outlasts the Feeling
illustrations.text: A young husband told me he no longer felt in love and wondered if that meant the marriage was over. I asked him what he thought a vow was for. We do not promise to keep feeling something, because no one can promise a feeling. We promise to keep acting in love when the feeling thins, precisely so that there is something holding the house up on the nights the warmth goes out. The vow was built for exactly the season he was in.
illustrations.point: Love is not mainly a feeling we fall into but a promise we keep. The vow was made for the seasons the feeling thins.

illustrations.title: The Bench at the End
illustrations.text: An old couple sat on a park bench not speaking, and a young man watched them, certain their silence meant their love had died. But sit a while and you see it differently. After fifty years there is a quiet that is not empty but full, two people who no longer need words to fill the air because the years have said everything. He reached over without looking and covered her hand with his. That was a whole language. The young man simply had not learned to read it.
illustrations.point: Long love grows quiet, and the quiet is not death but depth. The years say what words no longer need to.

illustrations.title: No Garden Tends Itself
illustrations.text: No one has ever planted a garden, walked away for a year, and returned to find it more beautiful than they left it. Gardens do not hold their ground when neglected. They surrender it, slowly, to weeds and drought, and the reclaiming is far harder than the daily tending would have been. A marriage is a garden in exactly this way. It does not stay good on its own. It goes to weeds the moment two people stop kneeling in the dirt of it.
illustrations.point: A marriage does not coast. Left untended it does not stay where it was but loses ground, and the recovery costs far more than the tending.

illustrations.title: He Knew the Name
illustrations.text: A man who had been married forty years was asked the secret, and he said it was that he had never stopped learning his wife's name. The questioner thought he had misheard. The man explained that the woman of forty years was not the bride of twenty. She had changed five times over, and so had he, and the work was to keep meeting the new person across the table rather than staying married to a memory of who she used to be.
illustrations.point: Faithfulness is not loyalty to who someone was. It is the daily work of meeting and loving the person they have become.

illustrations.title: The Thumb on the Scale
illustrations.text: An old merchant kept two sets of weights, a heavier one for buying and a lighter one for selling, and he prospered for years because no single customer ever weighed enough at once to notice. The fraud was invisible in any one transaction and devastating across a thousand of them. Scripture says God hates dishonest scales, and it is worth asking why so small a sin gets so strong a word. It is because the thumb on the scale always presses down on the one least able to push back.
illustrations.point: Injustice rarely announces itself. It works in small dishonest weights that fall hardest on those least able to resist, and God hates it for that reason.

illustrations.title: The Inconvenient Neighbor
illustrations.text: The priest and the Levite who passed the beaten man were not villains. They were busy, religious, on their way to do good things, and the man in the ditch was an interruption to a full day. The Samaritan was the one who let the suffering of a stranger derail his schedule and cost him his money and his time. The difference between them was not belief. It was whether mercy was allowed to be inconvenient.
illustrations.point: Justice is not mainly what we believe but what we let cost us. Mercy that is never inconvenient is not yet mercy.

illustrations.title: Going Upstream
illustrations.text: A village by a river kept pulling drowning people out of the water, day after day, growing skilled and tireless at the rescue. They built nets and trained swimmers and saved many. But no one walked upstream to ask who kept throwing people in. Charity pulls the bodies from the river. Justice walks upstream to stop the throwing. A church can be very busy with the first and never ask the second.
illustrations.point: Mercy rescues the suffering downstream. Justice goes upstream to ask why they are in the water. The kingdom requires both.

illustrations.title: The Widow at the Door
illustrations.text: Jesus told of a widow with no power, no money, and no one to speak for her, who wore down a corrupt judge simply by refusing to stop knocking. She had nothing but persistence and a just cause, and in the end the judge ruled for her just to be rid of the banging on his door. Jesus told it to teach us about prayer, but notice who the hero is. The one with no standing, who would not be quietly sent away.
illustrations.point: God hears the cry of the one the world will not listen to. The powerless who keep crying out for justice are heard in heaven.

illustrations.title: The Hundred and First Blow
illustrations.text: A stonecutter strikes a great block a hundred times and not a crack shows. He strikes it the hundred and first time, and it splits clean in two. He knows it was not that last blow that did it. It was all hundred that came before, every one of them working unseen in the stone while nothing on the surface seemed to change. The blow that finally breaks the stone gets the credit for the work of all the ones that looked like failures.
illustrations.point: Faithfulness that seems to accomplish nothing is working unseen. The breakthrough rests on the blows that looked wasted.

illustrations.title: The Wall at Mile Twenty
illustrations.text: Marathon runners speak of hitting the wall around mile twenty, when the body's easy fuel is spent and every remaining mile must be run on something deeper and harder to reach. The wall is not a sign that you are failing. It is the predictable place where the easy strength runs out and the real race begins. Many quit there, thinking the pain means they were not built for it, when the pain means only that they have reached the part where it counts.
illustrations.point: The point where the easy strength fails is not the sign to quit. It is the place the real race begins.

illustrations.title: Five Years Underground
illustrations.text: A certain bamboo is planted and watered and tended for years, and for a long season nothing breaks the surface of the soil. A farmer who did not know better would give up and call the seed dead. But underground it is building a root system vast and deep, and when at last it shoots up it can climb dozens of feet in a matter of weeks. The visible growth that astonishes everyone was bought by years of invisible growth that impressed no one.
illustrations.point: Long seasons where nothing shows are not wasted. God is building roots in the dark that the visible growth will one day require.

illustrations.title: The Candle Spends Itself
illustrations.text: A candle gives light only by being consumed. There is no way for it to shine and also keep all its wax. The light and the spending are the same act, and the candle that refused to be used up in order to preserve itself would simply sit in the dark, whole and useless. A life poured out in faithful service grows shorter in one sense even as it gives the only thing it was made to give.
illustrations.point: A faithful life gives light by being spent. The cost is not the enemy of the calling. It is the calling.

illustrations.title: The Lighthouse Holds Its Ground
illustrations.text: A lighthouse does not run up and down the coast chasing ships in trouble. It does one thing for decades. It stands in the same place through every storm and keeps its light burning, and ships set their course by it precisely because it never moves. Its power is its constancy. The world is full of people who want to do something dramatic and few who will simply stay in one place and keep the light lit for forty years.
illustrations.point: Faithfulness is often not dramatic action but unmoving constancy. The light that never wanders is the one others steer by.

illustrations.title: Salt That Forgot Its Job
illustrations.text: Salt does its work by disappearing into what it preserves. You do not taste good salt as a lump. You taste the food it has quietly saved from rot and made worth eating. Jesus warned of salt that loses its savor, salt that is still technically salt but has stopped doing the one thing salt is for. A faith that is still on the shelf but no longer working into the world around it has become exactly that, present and useless.
illustrations.point: A faith kept to itself and doing nothing in the world has lost the point of being faith at all. We are kept to be spent.
